10. The Question on the Woodcutter “Venerable Nāgasena, when you say that ‘two qualities of a woodcutter are to be adopted,’ which are those two qualities to be adopted?
“Just as, Great King, a woodcutter fells a tree by following the black line;”

In the same way, great king, a yogi, a practitioner of yoga, having brought himself into conformity with the teaching of the Conqueror and having established himself upon the earth of virtue, should cut away the defilements with the hand of faith, taking hold of the adze of wisdom.
This, great king, is the first quality of the carpenter that should be adopted.
Furthermore, great king, the carpenter, having removed the softwood, takes up the heartwood.
In the same way, Great King, when a practitioner, a follower of yoga, asserts eternalism, annihilationism, that the soul is the same as the body,

that the soul is one thing and the body another, that there is a supreme being other than the supreme, that things are uncreated and incapable of change, that there is no human effort, that the holy life is not lived,
that there is the destruction of beings, the manifestation of new beings, or that conditioned phenomena are eternal— then whoever performs such views experiences [the result] for themselves.
Having set aside such points of dispute as "one person acts, another experiences [the result]" and the views that there is a fruit of karma or a fruit of action,
one must adopt the intrinsic nature of formations— which is supreme emptiness, devoid of effort and devoid of a soul, and absolute emptiness.
This, Great King, is the second quality of the carpenter that should be adopted.
And this was said, Great King, by the Blessed One, the God above gods, in the Sutta Nipāta:
“Sweep away the kāraṇḍava weed.”
Cast away the refuse;
then drive out the chaff—
those who are not ascetics yet pride themselves on being ascetics.
Having expelled those of evil desires,
who follow evil conduct and haunts;
let the pure dwell in association with the pure.
“Live together with mindfulness;
then, being united and prudent,
you will make an end of suffering.”
The tenth question: On the Woodpecker.
The sixth chapter: On the Monkey.
Its summary verse:
The monkey, the boy, the tortoise,
the forest, and the tree as the fifth;
the cloud, the gem, and the hunter.
And as for the fisherman and the carpenter.
